Raskolnikov.description: The protagonist of the novel, a former student who commits a central murder and struggles with his conscience and legal consequences.

Alyona Ivanovna.description: The old pawnbroker with whom Raskolnikov does business; she is described as a suspicious, miserly woman and is the victim of the central murder.

S. Place.description: An abbreviated street or square name in St. Petersburg, typical of 19th-century Russian novels to obscure exact locations.

K. bridge.description: An abbreviated bridge name in St. Petersburg, following the convention of partial naming in Russian literature.

Petersburg.description: Short for St. Petersburg, the capital of imperial Russia at the time and the primary setting of the novel.

Hay Market.description: A well-known market area in St. Petersburg, associated with poverty, working-class life, and various establishments.

civil service.description: The government bureaucracy of imperial Russia, employing clerks and officials.

ikon.description: A religious image or painting, especially in the Russian Orthodox tradition, used for private devotion.

garret.description: A small, often cramped attic room, typically rented cheaply to poor tenants.

pot-houses.description: Cheap taverns or pubs where alcoholic drinks are served, often frequented by the lower classes.

waggon.description: A large, heavy cart used for transporting goods or people, typically drawn by horses.

dray horse.description: A strong horse used for pulling heavy loads, such as carts or wagons.

tenement.description: A building divided into small apartments or rooms, often rented by working-class or poor families.

flat.description: A British/Russian term for an apartment or set of rooms within a building.

pledge.description: An item left with a pawnbroker as security for a loan.

rouble.description: The basic unit of currency in Russia.

copeck.description: A subunit of the rouble; 100 copecks make one rouble.

muslin.description: A lightweight cotton fabric, often used for curtains or clothing.

strong-box.description: A sturdy, lockable box used for storing valuables or money.

tavern.description: An establishment where alcoholic drinks are served, similar to a pub or inn.

concertina.description: A small, accordion-like musical instrument popular in 19th-century Europe.

Marmeladov.description: A titular counsellor and alcoholic government clerk whose family lives in extreme poverty.

Katerina Ivanovna.description: Marmeladov's wife, an educated woman and officer's daughter, suffering from illness and poverty.

Darya Frantsovna.description: A woman of ill repute, known to the police, who played a role in Sonia's downfall.

Ivan Ivanitch Klopstock.description: A civil counsellor who mistreats Sonia by not paying her for her sewing work.

Amalia Fyodorovna Lippevechsel.description: The Marmeladovs' landlady, a German woman who manages the crowded and chaotic lodging house, often quarrelsome and at odds with Katerina Ivanovna.

Kapernaumov.description: A lame tailor with a cleft palate and his family, including his deaf wife, with whom Sonia lodges.

Ivan Afanasyvitch.description: A high-ranking official, referred to as 'his excellency,' who gives Marmeladov another chance in government service.

Neva.description: The main river running through St. Petersburg, Russia.

England.description: Referenced as a place where political economy and modern ideas influence social policy.

Bedlam.description: Originally a famous London mental asylum, here used to describe chaos and disorder.

Lewes’ Physiology.description: A reference to a scientific book by George Henry Lewes, an English philosopher and physiologist.

Cyrus of Persia.description: An ancient Persian king, mentioned as the point where Sonia's education ended.

Kozel.description: A cabinet-maker and owner of the house where the Marmeladovs live; the lodging house is referred to as Kozel’s house.

Egyptian bridge.description: A well-known bridge in St. Petersburg, used here as a landmark.

titular counsellor.description: A low-ranking civil service title in Imperial Russia, part of the Table of Ranks.

yellow passport.description: A document issued to registered prostitutes in Tsarist Russia, marking their social status and legal permission for prostitution.

drap de dames.description: A type of fine woolen fabric, often used for women's shawls.

chemise.description: A simple, loose-fitting undergarment or dress.

pelisse.description: A long, often fur-lined coat or cloak, fashionable in the 19th century.

pomatum.description: A scented ointment or pomade used for styling hair.

farthing.description: A very small unit of currency, used here to indicate a trivial sum.

cabinet-maker.description: A skilled craftsman who makes fine furniture.

tallow-candle.description: A candle made from animal fat, common among the poor in the 19th century.

American leather.description: A type of imitation leather used for cheap furniture coverings.

Nastasya.description: Nastasya is the cook and only servant in Raskolnikov's lodging house, a talkative country peasant-woman who sometimes brings him food and cleans his room.

Praskovya Pavlovna.description: Raskolnikov's landlady who is frustrated by his debt; she was once the mother of his deceased fiancée, Natalya Yegorovna.

Vassilyevsky Prospect.description: A major street or avenue on Vassilyevsky Island in St. Petersburg.

Senate.description: Refers to the Governing Senate, the highest judicial and administrative body in Imperial Russia.

Our Lady.description: A reference to the Virgin Mary, often invoked in Russian Orthodox prayers and religious observances.

roubles.description: The basic unit of currency in Russia.

pension.description: A regular payment made by the government to someone who is retired or otherwise eligible, often due to service or age.

governess.description: A woman employed to teach and care for children in a private household.

regimental.description: Relating to a military regiment; here, refers to Svidrigaïlov's old habits from his time in the army.

Bacchus.description: The Roman god of wine; used here to refer to drunkenness.

versts.description: A Russian unit of distance, approximately 1.07 kilometers or about two-thirds of a mile.

third class.description: The cheapest class of travel on Russian trains, with minimal comfort.

bureau.description: An office or agency, especially one dealing with legal or governmental matters.

civil and commercial litigation.description: Legal proceedings relating to non-criminal (civil) and business (commercial) disputes.

landlady.description: A woman who owns and rents out rooms or apartments to tenants.

Svidrigaïlov.description: Dounia's former employer, a morally ambiguous and mysterious figure who follows the Raskolnikov family to St. Petersburg.

Razumihin.description: Raskolnikov's loyal and good-natured friend from university who provides constant support to Raskolnikov and his family.

Holy Mother of Kazan.description: An icon of the Virgin Mary, highly venerated in Russian Orthodoxy, often kept in homes for protection and prayer.

Golgotha.description: The hill outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, used metaphorically for great suffering or sacrifice.

Anna.description: Refers to the Order of St. Anna, a Russian imperial honor awarded for civil or military merit.

Schleswig-Holstein.description: A region in northern Europe, referenced here as a symbol of something grand and unattainable.

K—— Boulevard.description: A partially anonymized street name, typical in Russian literature to indicate a real or fictional location in St. Petersburg.

Darya Frantsovnas.description: Refers to women like Darya Frantsovna, a common type of landlady or matron in Russian society, often associated with gossip and moral policing.

university.description: Refers to the institution of higher education attended by Raskolnikov and Razumihin, likely St. Petersburg University.

express.description: A fast means of travel, such as an express train or carriage.

peasant’s cart.description: A simple, horse-drawn vehicle used by Russian peasants for transportation.

sacking.description: Coarse woven material, such as burlap, used for covering or packing.

verst.description: A Russian unit of distance, approximately 1.07 kilometers or about two-thirds of a mile.

paper ones.description: Paper roubles, as opposed to silver coins; refers to paper currency.

knits woollen shawls.description: A reference to making woolen garments by hand, a common way for poor women to earn extra money.

Schilleresque.description: Resembling the idealism and noble sentimentality found in the works of German writer Friedrich Schiller.

orders of merit.description: Official honors or decorations awarded for distinguished service.

buttonhole.description: A slit in the lapel of a coat where a decoration or flower may be worn.

nigger.description: An offensive and outdated term for a Black person, reflecting the period's language and attitudes.

Lett.description: An archaic term for a Latvian person.

concubine.description: A woman who lives with a man but has lower status than his wife or wives.

casuists.description: People skilled in resolving moral problems by the application of theoretical rules.

Jesuitical.description: Subtly or excessively argumentative or scheming, often with a connotation of moral flexibility.

copecks.description: A small unit of Russian currency, one hundredth of a rouble.

cab.description: A horse-drawn carriage for hire, used for transportation in cities.

gentlefolk.description: People of good birth or social standing; gentry.

percentage.description: Here, used cynically to refer to a portion of people expected to fall into vice or ruin, as if it were a statistical inevitability.

comrades.description: Fellow students or colleagues, often used in Russian to denote friendship or solidarity.

Pushkin.description: Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin was a famous Russian poet and writer, referenced here as a symbol of artistic genius.

Turgenev.description: Ivan Sergeyevich Turgenev was a renowned Russian novelist and playwright, mentioned as an example of an artist.

Lizaveta Ivanovna.description: Lizaveta Ivanovna is the meek, submissive, and much-abused younger (step)sister of Alyona Ivanovna, the pawnbroker, and is responsible for the cleanliness of Alyona's flat.

Matvey.description: Matvey is briefly mentioned as the driver of the bay horse, referenced by Mikolka in the dream.

Lesser Neva.description: A branch of the Neva River in St. Petersburg.

Petrovsky Ostrov.description: Another island in St. Petersburg, known for its greenery and summer villas.

Ivanovna.description: A Russian patronymic meaning 'daughter of Ivan,' used as part of formal address.

vodka.description: A traditional Russian distilled alcoholic beverage, clear and strong.

balalaïka.description: A traditional Russian stringed musical instrument with a triangular body, commonly used in folk music.

cupola.description: A small dome, often found atop Russian Orthodox churches.

ikons.description: Religious images or paintings, especially in the Eastern Orthodox tradition, used for veneration.

mass.description: A religious service, particularly in the Christian tradition; in Russia, refers to the Orthodox liturgy.

huckster.description: A small-scale vendor or peddler, often selling goods in the street or market.

costermongers.description: Street sellers of fruit, vegetables, or other goods, typically from a barrow or cart.

barrows.description: Handcarts used by street vendors to display and transport their goods.

verandahs.description: Roofed, open-air porches or galleries attached to the outside of a building.

nag.description: A term for a small, old, or worn-out horse, often used disparagingly.

tambourine.description: A small handheld percussion instrument with jingling metal disks, used in folk music.

Pokorev.description: A student acquaintance of Raskolnikov who previously gave him Alyona Ivanovna's address.

the huckster.description: A local dealer or trader who, along with his wife, employs Lizaveta to sell household goods.

the officer.description: A young officer who listens to the student's conversation about Alyona Ivanovna and Lizaveta in the tavern.

the student.description: An unnamed student who discusses Alyona Ivanovna and Lizaveta in the tavern, expressing radical ideas about morality and murder.

the porter.description: A man responsible for watching over the entrance and common areas of the building where Raskolnikov lives.

Harkov.description: A city in Ukraine (now spelled Kharkiv), referenced as the place where Pokorev has gone.

monastery.description: A religious institution where monks live; in this context, Alyona Ivanovna intends to leave her money to a monastery for prayers after her death.

province of N——.description: A purposely obscured location, typical in Russian literature, indicating an unspecified province.

Lock hospitals.description: Hospitals in 19th-century Russia (and Britain) specializing in the treatment of venereal diseases.

summer garden.description: A famous park in St. Petersburg, known for its fountains and statues.

field of Mars.description: A large open space in central St. Petersburg, historically used for military parades and public gatherings.

Mihailovsky Palace.description: A grand palace in St. Petersburg, now housing the Russian Museum.

movables.description: Personal property that can be moved, such as furniture.

charwoman.description: A woman employed to do cleaning or other menial work in someone else's house.

noose.description: A loop with a running knot, used here as a device to carry the axe discreetly.

porter.description: A person employed to look after the entrance of a building and assist tenants or visitors.

Koch.description: Koch is a minor character, a man who comes to visit Alyona Ivanovna on business and later discovers something is wrong at her flat.

Mitka.description: Mitka is mentioned in a shouted warning; likely a workman or porter, though his role here is only as a name called out during the commotion.

Gambrinus.description: A billiard hall or tavern referenced as a place where Koch and the young man played billiards.

Cyprus.description: Refers to Cyprus wood, a material used for one of the crosses found on the old woman; Cyprus wood was considered special or sacred in Russian Orthodoxy.

chamois.description: A type of soft, pliable leather, often used for purses or cleaning cloths.

filigree.description: Delicate ornamental work made from fine gold or silver wire.

gateway.description: An entrance passage or archway into a courtyard or building, typical in Russian city architecture.

Luise Ivanovna.description: Luise Ivanovna is a gaily-dressed, stout woman with a German accent who appears at the police office, involved in a scandal at her lodging house.

Ilya Petrovitch.description: Ilya Petrovitch is the assistant superintendent at the police station, known for his explosive temper and brusque manner.

Nikodim Fomitch.description: The superintendent of the district police, described as friendly and civil despite his nickname.

Alexandr Grigorievitch.description: The head clerk at the police office who becomes suspicious of Raskolnikov's behavior.

Pestryakov.description: Pestryakov is a student mentioned as a witness in the murder investigation, seen at the gate with friends.

police office.description: The government office where police business is conducted, including investigations and administrative matters.

district police-station.description: The local police headquarters responsible for law enforcement in a specific area of the city.

district superintendent.description: The chief officer in charge of a district police-station.

the province of X.description: A generic reference to a Russian province, used to anonymize the location of Raskolnikov's family.

Noah’s Ark.description: A biblical reference used metaphorically to describe a crowded, chaotic house with many different people.

house of correction.description: A detention facility or prison for minor offenders or those awaiting trial.

regiment.description: A military unit, here referring to Ilya Petrovitch's former service.

taverns.description: Drinking establishments or bars, common in 19th-century Russia.

mourning.description: The practice of wearing black or somber clothing to signify grief after a death.

curtsying.description: A formal gesture of respect performed by women, involving a slight bending of the knees and lowering of the body.

cockaded cap.description: A hat decorated with a cockade, a knot of ribbons or similar ornament, often part of a uniform.

I O U.description: A written acknowledgment of debt, standing for 'I owe you.'

writ.description: A formal written order issued by a legal authority.

lock-up.description: A temporary holding cell or jail.

cad.description: A man who behaves dishonorably, especially toward women.

pianoforte.description: An early term for the piano.

sein rock.description: German for 'his coat'; used here in the context of a damaged garment.

thanksgiving service.description: A religious service held to give thanks, often after a fortunate escape or event.

crossing himself.description: A Christian gesture of making the sign of the cross for protection or blessing.

Heruvimov.description: Heruvimov is a bookseller and publisher who employs Razumihin to translate works and pays him for his services.

Ekaterininsky Canal.description: A canal in St. Petersburg, Russia, often referenced in the novel as a location near Raskolnikov's lodgings.

V—— Prospect.description: A partially redacted name for a major avenue (prospect) in St. Petersburg, typical of Dostoevsky's style to obscure exact locations.

Islands.description: Refers to the group of islands in the Neva delta, a quieter, more remote part of St. Petersburg.

Les Confessions.description: A famous autobiographical work by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, referenced here as a source for translation.

Radishchev.description: Alexander Radishchev, a Russian writer and social critic, known for his radical ideas; mentioned as a comparison to Rousseau.

Nikolaevsky Bridge.description: A bridge in St. Petersburg crossing the Neva River, known today as the Annunciation Bridge.

palace.description: Refers to one of the grand palaces along the Neva, likely the Winter Palace, a symbol of imperial Russia.

cathedral.description: Refers to the main church in a Russian town or city, often the site of important religious ceremonies; most likely refers to St. Isaac's Cathedral, a prominent landmark in St. Petersburg.

signature.description: In publishing, a 'signature' is a section of printed sheets folded together, often used as a unit for payment in translation or printing work.

greatcoat.description: A heavy overcoat, typically worn in 19th-century Russia for warmth.

Zossimov.description: A doctor and friend of Razumihin, who attends to Raskolnikov during his illness and testifies to his mental and physical condition.

messenger.description: A young man from the office of the merchant Shelopaev, who brings Raskolnikov a remittance.

Alexey Semyonovitch.description: An employee at the office who previously delivered a remittance to Raskolnikov.

Afanasy Ivanovitch Vahrushin.description: A merchant from Raskolnikov's hometown who facilitates money transfers from Raskolnikov's mother.

Semyon Semyonovitch.description: An employee at the office who receives instructions from Vahrushin regarding the remittance.

Natalya Yegorovna.description: Praskovya Pavlovna's deceased daughter, once engaged to Raskolnikov.

Mr. Tchebarov.description: A businessman who acquired Raskolnikov's IOU and previously attempted to court Praskovya Pavlovna.

Tolstyakov.description: A friend of Razumihin, mentioned in an anecdote about hats.

Five Corners.description: A district or intersection in St. Petersburg known for its distinctive layout and buildings.

Harlamov’s house.description: A lodging house in the Five Corners area, previously associated with Raskolnikov.

Buch’s.description: Another lodging house, confused with Harlamov’s by Razumihin.

address bureau.description: A municipal office in St. Petersburg where residents' addresses are registered and can be looked up.

General Kobelev.description: A general mentioned as being untraceable at the address bureau, likely as an example.

Krestovsky Island.description: An island in St. Petersburg, referenced by Raskolnikov in his delirium.

United States of America.description: Mentioned humorously by Razumihin when discussing trousers, reflecting the period's awareness of America.

English Embassy.description: The diplomatic mission of England in St. Petersburg; Razumihin buys boots previously owned by its secretary.

Fedyaev’s.description: A shop known for selling second-hand clothing, mentioned by Razumihin.

Sharmer’s.description: A clothing shop referenced by Razumihin, likely known for overcoats.

remittance.description: A sum of money sent, especially by mail, as payment or a gift.

faculty.description: Used here to mean the medical faculty or doctors, referring to their permission or advice.

linen.description: Refers to underclothes or shirts, not just fabric.

breeches.description: Trousers, especially those reaching to the knee or just below.

Palmerston.description: A nickname for Raskolnikov's battered old hat, possibly referencing Lord Palmerston, a British statesman, as a joke.

tryst.description: A private, romantic rendezvous or meeting, used here humorously.

bundle.description: A package or parcel, often of clothing or belongings.

Porfiry Petrovitch.description: Porfiry Petrovitch is the head of the Investigation Department and a distant relation of Razumihin, involved in the investigation of the pawnbroker's murder.

Dushkin.description: A peasant and pawnbroker who owns a dram-shop and brought the jeweller’s case to the police, suspecting Nikolay.

Nikolay.description: A journeyman house-painter who, out of fear and religious delirium, confesses to the murder he did not commit.

Dmitri.description: A house-painter and coworker of Nikolay, present at the scene on the day of the murder.

Afanasy Pavlovitch.description: A man mentioned by Nikolay as the person from whom he first heard about the murder.

Kryukov.description: A man who was seen entering the building at the time of the murder, mentioned as a witness.

Palais de Cristal.description: A fashionable restaurant or entertainment venue in St. Petersburg, popular in the 19th century.

Investigation Department.description: The police department responsible for criminal investigations, headed by Porfiry Petrovitch.

Zaraïsk.description: A province and district in Russia, the home region of Dushkin and Nikolay.

Ryazan.description: A region in Russia from which Dushkin and Nikolay originate.

Peski.description: A district or area in St. Petersburg, mentioned as a place where Nikolay stayed.

Kolomensky men.description: Workmen from the Kolomna district of St. Petersburg, with whom Nikolay claims to have stayed.

note.description: A paper currency or banknote, here referring to a rouble note.

pledges.description: Items left with a pawnbroker as security for a loan.

unredeemed pledges.description: Items pawned but not reclaimed by their owners, often sold by pawnbrokers.

dram-shop.description: A small bar or tavern where alcoholic drinks are sold, especially cheap spirits, often associated with lower-class clientele.

spree.description: A period of unrestrained drinking or partying.

entry.description: The entrance or hallway of a building.

jewel-case.description: A small box for holding jewelry, central to the evidence in the murder case.

prosecution.description: The legal party responsible for presenting the case against the accused in a criminal trial.

circumstantial evidence.description: Evidence that relies on inference rather than direct observation, often used in legal contexts.

Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov.description: A young clerk in the Ministry and Luzhin’s acquaintance who holds radical, modern ideas and lodges in the same house as the Marmeladovs.

Bakaleyev’s house.description: A lodging house near Raskolnikov’s residence, where Luzhin has found rooms for Raskolnikov’s mother and sister; Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia are staying there.

Voskresensky.description: A district or street in Saint Petersburg, where Bakaleyev’s house is located.

Yushin.description: A merchant who owns and lets rooms in Bakaleyev’s house.

Ministry.description: Refers to a government department; Lebeziatnikov is a clerk in one of the ministries.

Moscow.description: The capital city of Russia, mentioned as the site of recent criminal activity.

the police office.description: Refers to the local police station or headquarters in Saint Petersburg.

the provinces.description: Refers to areas of Russia outside the capital, often considered less progressive or modern.

fiancé.description: A man engaged to be married.

betrothed.description: A person to whom one is engaged to be married.

pawnbroker.description: A person who lends money at interest in exchange for personal property left as security.

trunks.description: Large, sturdy boxes or chests used for storing clothes and personal belongings.

lodging.description: A rented room or rooms, typically in someone else's house.

Duclida.description: Duclida is a young street woman who interacts with Raskolnikov, asking him for money.

Alyoshka.description: Alyoshka is the younger of two workmen papering the walls in the murdered pawnbroker's flat.

Afrosinya.description: Afrosinya is a local woman who attempts suicide by drowning, recognized by a bystander.

Potchinkov.description: Potchinkov is the owner of the house where Razumihin is having his house-warming, referenced as a location.

Babushkin.description: Babushkin is the owner of the flat where Razumihin lives, mentioned as an address; the flat itself is referenced as Babushkin’s flat.

Sadovy Street.description: A street in St. Petersburg, part of the district where Raskolnikov wanders.

Moscow News.description: A newspaper published in Moscow, referenced for news of crimes.

Shil’s house.description: The building where Raskolnikov lives, identified by the name of its owner.

Potchinkov’s house.description: The building where Razumihin lives and is hosting a house-warming party.

X—— Bridge.description: A bridge in St. Petersburg, the exact name obscured, where Raskolnikov witnesses a suicide attempt.

gymnasium.description: In Russia, a type of secondary school with a classical curriculum, indicating Zametov's level of education.

samovar.description: A traditional Russian metal urn used to boil water for tea.

crinoline.description: A stiffened or structured petticoat designed to hold out a woman's skirt, fashionable in the 19th century.

mantle.description: A loose, sleeveless cloak or shawl, worn as outer clothing.

barrel organ.description: A mechanical musical instrument that plays tunes by turning a handle, often used by street performers to collect money.

corn chandler.description: A dealer in corn or grain.

district.description: In the Russian context, a smaller administrative division within a province.

eating-house.description: A simple restaurant or tavern serving food and drink.

saloon.description: A public room or tavern for drinking and entertainment.

fashion book.description: A publication with illustrations of the latest clothing styles, used by tailors and dressmakers.

spermaceti ointment.description: A salve made from spermaceti, a waxy substance from whales, used for medicinal or cosmetic purposes.

lymph.description: A reference to the clear bodily fluid, here used metaphorically to suggest lack of vitality.

storey.description: A level or floor of a building.

parapet.description: A low protective wall along the edge of a roof, bridge, or balcony.

Polenka.description: The eldest daughter of Katerina Ivanovna and Marmeladov, a caring child who assists her mother.

Lida.description: The youngest daughter of Marmeladov and Katerina Ivanovna, described as a small, sickly girl.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna Raskolnikov.description: Pulcheria Alexandrovna Raskolnikov is Raskolnikov's devoted and emotional mother, deeply concerned for her son's well-being.

Princess Bezzemelny.description: A noblewoman mentioned by Katerina Ivanovna as a figure from her past social life.

Prince Schegolskoy.description: A nobleman and kammerjunker mentioned by Katerina Ivanovna as a former suitor.

kammerjunker.description: A junior court title in Imperial Russia, roughly equivalent to a gentleman-in-waiting.

Governor-General.description: The highest civil authority in a Russian province, referenced as someone Katerina Ivanovna threatens to inform.

samovars.description: Traditional Russian metal urns used to boil water for tea.

kerchief.description: A square piece of cloth worn on the head or around the neck.

Ave Maria.description: A traditional Christian prayer addressed to the Virgin Mary, recited here by the children.

Luzhin.description: Dounia's wealthy, self-important, and manipulative suitor whose proposed marriage creates central conflict.

Rubinstein.description: Anton Rubinstein was a famous 19th-century Russian pianist and composer, used here as a reference to musical skill.

Prussian House of Lords.description: A legislative body in the Kingdom of Prussia, referenced humorously in conversation.

Number 3.description: Refers to a specific apartment or room number in the building, known for a previous scandal.

lodgings.description: Rented rooms or accommodations, often used by students and the poor in Russian cities.

maître.description: French for 'master,' used here to mean an accomplished performer or expert.

powder.description: A form of medicine, often administered in powdered form in 19th-century Russia.

delirium.description: A disturbed state of mind, often due to illness, characterized by confusion and agitation.

monomania.description: An obsession with a single idea or subject, considered a form of mental illness in the 19th century.

integral calculus.description: A branch of mathematics dealing with integrals, referenced humorously as a subject for teaching.

feather bed.description: A mattress filled with feathers, considered a luxury and symbolizing comfort.

pailfuls.description: Buckets full; a pail is a bucket, so 'pailfuls' means several buckets' worth.

gutter.description: A channel at the edge of a street for carrying off rainwater, often associated with dirt or lowliness.

St. Petersburg.description: The capital city of Imperial Russia at the time, where the events of the novel take place.

Venetian.description: Refers to Venice, Italy; here, a 'Venetian chain' describes a style of jewelry chain, indicating a foreign luxury item.

levées.description: Formal receptions or gatherings, often held by royalty or high society, where people pay their respects.

pothouse.description: A slang term for a cheap tavern or drinking establishment.

monomaniac.description: A person obsessed with a single idea or subject.

hypochondriac.description: A person excessively worried about their health, often imagining illnesses.

circumstantial.description: Detailed and specific, often referring to evidence or accounts.

Vasya.description: A messenger boy in Afanasy Ivanitch’s shop, mentioned in comparison to Raskolnikov’s attire.

Afanasy Ivanitch.description: Owner of a shop where Vasya, the messenger boy, works; mentioned in passing.

Lieutenant Potanchikov.description: A deceased friend of Raskolnikov’s father, referenced as a cautionary tale about illness.

Marfa Petrovna Svidrigaïlov.description: Marfa Petrovna Svidrigaïlov is the wife of Mr. Svidrigaïlov, whose sudden death is discussed and who initially blames Dounia for her husband's advances but later publicly vindicates her.

Afanasy Ivanitch’s shop.description: A shop owned by Afanasy Ivanitch, referenced in relation to Vasya, the messenger boy.

court-yard.description: An open area within or adjacent to a building, common in Russian urban architecture.

Pyotr Petrovitch’s letter.description: A letter written by Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin to Dounia and her mother, which becomes a point of discussion.

the courts.description: Refers to the Russian legal system and its formal, bureaucratic language.

bath-house.description: A public facility for bathing, common in Russian culture, sometimes used for medical treatments.

consumption.description: An old term for tuberculosis, a serious infectious disease affecting the lungs.

alms.description: Charitable donations, usually of money or food, given to the poor.

nunnery.description: A convent or religious community for women (nuns).

stroke.description: A sudden medical condition where poor blood flow to the brain results in cell death, often leading to paralysis or death.

crossing herself.description: A gesture made by Orthodox Christians (and others), tracing the shape of a cross over the body as a sign of faith or to ward off evil.

Crevez, chiens, si vous n’êtes pas conte.description: French for 'Die, dogs, if you are not satisfied,' used here to express contempt for those dissatisfied with charity.

legal jargon.description: Specialized language used in legal documents and proceedings, often difficult for laypeople to understand.

parasol.description: A light umbrella used to provide shade from the sun, often carried by women in the 19th century.

Egypt.description: Referenced as the site of Napoleon's military campaign.

æsthetic.description: Relating to beauty or artistic taste; here used in a self-mocking way.

louse.description: An insult meaning a despicable or insignificant person; also refers to the small parasitic insect.

prophet.description: Used here to refer to a religious or revolutionary leader who claims divine authority.

sabre.description: A curved sword, often associated with cavalry or military figures.

battery.description: A group of artillery guns; here, metaphorically, a display of force.

Prince Svirbey.description: Prince Svirbey is mentioned as a distant relation of Svidrigaïlov and a personage of some importance.

America.description: A country mentioned as a possible destination for elopement, representing escape and new beginnings.

Nezhin.description: A town in Russia, mentioned as the origin of the Greek who caused Svidrigaïlov's imprisonment for debt.

Yusupov Garden.description: A public garden in St. Petersburg, named after the wealthy Yusupov family, mentioned as the site of a planned balloon ascent.

Malaya Vishera.description: A station referenced as the place where Svidrigaïlov claims to have seen Marfa Petrovna's ghost.

North Pole.description: The northernmost point on Earth, mentioned humorously as a possible destination.

French.description: Referenced in the phrase 'bonne guerre,' indicating a French expression.

German.description: Referenced in the story about a German woman who was thrashed by a nobleman.

apoplexy.description: A sudden loss of consciousness, often due to a stroke or cerebral hemorrhage.

serf.description: A peasant in 19th-century Russia who was legally bound to the land and the landowner.

card-sharper.description: A person who cheats at cards; a card cheat.

wedlock.description: The state of being married; marriage.

cookshop.description: A small restaurant or shop selling cooked food, often cheaply.

name-day.description: A celebration in Russian culture of the feast day of the saint after whom a person is named.

pour vous plaire.description: French for 'to please you' or 'for your pleasure.'

bonne guerre.description: French for 'fair game,' meaning a legitimate or acceptable trick or ruse.

Mother Russia.description: A personification of Russia, emphasizing its vastness and national character.

serfdom.description: The system of agricultural servitude in Russia, abolished in 1861, under which peasants were tied to the land and their landlords.

conjugal.description: Relating to marriage or the relationship between married partners.

legacy.description: Money or property left to someone in a will.

pawn.description: To deposit an item as security for a loan, with the item to be forfeited if the loan is not repaid.

canal.description: Refers to the St. Petersburg canal, a common feature of the city's geography and often associated with poverty and despair in the novel.

Jesus.description: Central figure of Christianity, believed to be the Son of God; his miracle of raising Lazarus is recounted in this chapter.

Mary.description: Another biblical character, sister of Lazarus and Martha, present at the miracle described in the Gospel of John.

gallery.description: A corridor or passage, often running along the side of a building or around a courtyard.

bedstead.description: The framework of a bed, typically without a mattress or bedding.

deal.description: A type of cheap, soft wood (usually pine or fir) commonly used for furniture in 19th-century Russia.

pedlar.description: A person who travels from place to place selling small goods, often door-to-door or in the streets.

graveclothes.description: Cloth wrappings used to dress a body for burial, as mentioned in the biblical story of Lazarus.

department of the investigation of crimi.description: A governmental office responsible for investigating criminal cases in 19th-century Russia.

sedentary.description: Describes a lifestyle or occupation involving much sitting and little physical activity.

incognito.description: A Latin term meaning 'in disguise' or 'with one's identity concealed'.

belfry.description: A bell tower, either attached to a church or standing alone.

decanter.description: A vessel used to hold and pour liquids, typically wine or water.

police station.description: The local law enforcement office where suspects and witnesses are questioned; a key location in the investigation.

warder.description: A prison guard or jailer responsible for overseeing prisoners.

scaffold.description: A raised platform used for executions, especially hangings; here, it symbolizes impending punishment.

memorial dinner.description: A traditional meal held after a funeral in Russian culture to honor the deceased.

senate.description: Refers to the Russian Senate, the highest judicial and administrative body in Imperial Russia.

Knopp’s.description: A fashionable shop in Petersburg, likely selling luxury goods and trousseau items.

English shop.description: A store in Petersburg known for selling imported English goods, considered prestigious.

France.description: Mentioned in the context of workmen’s associations, referencing French socialist movements.

trousseau.description: A collection of clothes and personal possessions a bride brings to her marriage.

lodgers.description: People who rent rooms in someone else's house, a common arrangement in 19th-century Russia.

commune.description: A collective living arrangement based on socialist principles, popular among Russian radicals.

memorial dinners.description: Feasts held in memory of the deceased, a Russian Orthodox custom.

subscription.description: A collection of money from multiple people for a charitable cause.

official.description: A government employee or civil servant in Imperial Russia.

bazaar.description: A market or marketplace, often used in Russian cities for buying food and provisions.

order.description: A chivalric or honorary order, indicating a high social or military distinction in Russia.

governor.description: A high-ranking official in charge of a province or city in Russia.

rice and honey.description: Traditional Russian dishes often served at memorial meals.

governor-general.description: A high-ranking official in the Russian imperial administration, often the head of a large region or city such as St. Petersburg.

commissariat clerk.description: A government official responsible for supplies or administration, present among the crowd.

bread and salt.description: A traditional symbol of hospitality in Russian culture.

atheists.description: People who do not believe in the existence of God; used here as an insult or accusation.

agitators.description: People who stir up public feeling or incite others, especially for political reasons.

office.description: Refers to the police or magistrate's office where official business and interrogations take place.

journal.description: A periodical publication; here, it refers to the publication in which Raskolnikov's article appeared.

yellow note.description: A colloquial term for a high-denomination Russian banknote, often yellow in color.

æsthetics.description: The branch of philosophy dealing with beauty and artistic taste, often spelled 'aesthetics' in modern English.

oraison funèbre.description: French for 'funeral oration', a speech in praise of someone who has died.

mamma.description: An affectionate or childish term for mother.

papa.description: An affectionate or childish term for father.

cancan.description: A lively, high-kicking dance originating in France, considered risqué in the 19th century.

den.description: A slang term for a disreputable or low-class establishment.

la nature et la vérité.description: French for 'nature and truth', suggesting authenticity.

assez causé.description: French for 'enough talk' or 'that’s enough conversation'.

vis-à-vis.description: French for 'face to face' or 'opposite', often used in dance to indicate partners.

orphan asylums.description: Institutions for the care and housing of orphaned children.

chronicle.description: A historical account of events arranged in chronological order.

capsule.description: In firearms, a small container holding the primer for igniting the gunpowder in a cartridge.

charge.description: A quantity of explosive or ammunition loaded into a firearm.

Russian.description: Refers to the world of Russian thought and society, highlighting the national context of the novel.

cross.description: A Christian religious symbol, often worn as a pendant for protection or devotion.
